name: Hair texture powder / sea salt spray

lead: Sea salt spray and texture powder are styling products that add volume, grip and a matte, tousled look. Sea salt spray is a salt-and-water mist applied to damp hair, and texture powder is a fine dry powder dusted at the roots.

Styling products generally coat or swell the strand to create temporary body, and the change is visible immediately after styling. Some users say the salt spray also adds waviness, and people on looksmax.org share homemade versions. No clinical studies of either product type were found.

paras: People spray salt mist onto damp hair and scrunch or blow-dry, or dust powder at the roots and work it through dry hair with their fingers. They are used on styling days and washed out afterward. Powder is often layered under a hold product.
Styling products can dry hair or build up, causing dullness or breakage, according to Wikipedia. No safety studies specific to these two product types were found.

angle.text: Sea salt spray and texture powder add volume, grip and a matte, tousled finish you can see as soon as you style. Salt mist is applied to damp hair and powder dusted dry at the roots; some users also say the spray makes hair wavier.

lead: Texture powders and sea salt sprays are hair styling products used to make hair look fuller, grippier and more tousled, with a matte, lived-in finish rather than a shiny, slicked one. Sea salt spray is a salt-and-water mist applied to damp hair to encourage waves and body, while texture powder is a fine dry powder dusted at the roots to add lift and hold [1][2][3].

Wikipedia's article on styling products explains that volumisers add temporary volume, body and shine to thin or flat hair, with humectants swelling the strand and polymers coating it, and that mousse can add texture for a beach-blown effect [1]. A dedicated Wikipedia article on hair texture powder describes modern formulas as lightweight powders, often based on silica or rice starch, that add body and separation without a sticky or stiff feel, in volumising, matte and texturising variants [3]. No clinical studies of either product were found.

For people with thinning or fine hair, these products are a cosmetic way to look like they have more density at the front and crown. On looksmax.org, members share homemade sea salt sprays and discuss them for adding waviness and curl [2].
infobox: Silica, rice starch and other fine powders [3]
Starch or flour hair powder, late 1500s onward [3]

paras: General styling products work by coating strands with polymers, wax or oil, or by swelling the strand with humectants [1]. Volumisers are described as products that add temporary volume and body to thin or flat hair, available as shampoo, conditioner, spray, pomade or lotion, and are typically applied to damp roots and blow-dried [1]. Sea salt sprays and texture powders sit in that wider category; their formulations vary by brand.

Mousse, a lighter foam than gel, can add volume and shine and is also used to define curls or create a beach-blown texture on damp hair [1]. Sea salt spray is the more direct version of that beach look, a liquid applied to damp hair and left to dry, often finished by scrunching or blow-drying, which is how forum users describe using it [2].

Texture powders are dry formulas shaken or dusted onto the roots and mid-lengths. According to Wikipedia, they are popular for adding root volume, which suits fine or thinning hair, and for giving hold and definition without the stiffness of hair spray or gel. Volumising powders lift the roots, matte powders reduce shine, and texturising powders add grit for a tousled look [3].

They are related to dry shampoo, a powder product usually sold in aerosol cans whose starch absorbs scalp oil; Wikipedia notes dry shampoo can also add volume, help tease hair and substitute for mousse [4]. Wikipedia lists possible side effects of dry shampoo, including follicle inflammation, dermatitis and residue build-up, and the oil and powder stay on the scalp until a wash [4].

Powder in the hair is far older than modern styling products. Powdered starch or flour was used on wigs and natural hair as early as the late 1500s and early 1600s, hair powder was a status symbol among the upper classes in France and England in the 18th century, and its use declined after the French Revolution as natural styles came into fashion and taxes were placed on it [3].

Modern styling products have their own chronology: Chase Products first packaged hair spray in the US in 1948, hair spray became the best-selling beauty product on the market by 1964, and the 1980s punk movement popularised gel for spiky styles [1][5]. Hair gel and waxy styling agents are traced to the ancient Egyptians and Gauls [1][6].

For people who are growing out their hair or have fine or thinning hair, texture products are a low-commitment way to change how the hairstyle reads in photos and in person: adding lift at the crown, separating strands and removing shine. They are also used with wavy or curly hair to emphasise the pattern.

One looksmax.org thread presents a homemade version of sea salt spray, using water, salt and a little olive oil in a spray bottle, applied to hair after washing and scrunched in to encourage curl [2]. The author reports tighter curls afterwards, while another user replies that the hair was already curly [2].

Wikipedia notes that most styling products do not damage hair when applied properly, but any product can dry hair, and some ingredients can strip oils or build up and cause dullness, dryness, breakage, eczema or thinning [1]. Conditioning overviews describe heat, bleaching and weathering as separate sources of damage that strip the cuticle's lipid layer [7]. Aerosol powders and dry shampoos carry flammability and inhalation considerations noted for the category [4].

lore.intro: Sea salt spray appears in hair-texture threads, including a do-it-yourself recipe presented as a cheaper alternative to commercial sprays [2].
